comments.content: Ignoring the whole `.vscode` directory at the repo root conflicts with the existing intent in `client/.gitignore`, which un-ignores `.vscode/extensions.json` (`!.vscode/extensions.json`) so recommended extensions can be shared. Git does not descend into ignored directories, so a file inside the now-excluded `client/.vscode/` can never be re-included by the negation rule and that rule becomes dead code. Use a pattern that ignores the contents rather than the directory (e.g. `.vscode/*`) if sharing `extensions.json` is still desired; also add the missing trailing newline.

Wait — order/precedence: patterns in higher-level `.gitignore` (root) are applied first; lower-level (client/.gitignore) patterns override them. But the rule about not re-including files inside excluded directories applies: "It is not possible to re-include a file if a parent directory of that file is excluded." Root `.gitignore` excluding `.vscode` (directory) excludes the directory `client/.vscode`, so files within cannot be re-included by client/.gitignore's `!.vscode/extensions.json`.

Git doesn't list excluded directories for performance reasons, so any patterns on contained files have no effect, no matter where they are defined."

The third alternative `[a-f0-9]{12,64}` is unreachable: every string it can match (12–64 hex chars) is already matched by the earlier `[a-zA-Z0-9]+` alternative, since Joi's `regex()` is unanchored alternation over the whole value. This is effectively dead validation logic that also gives a false impression that short hex IDs are restricted to 12–64 chars. The pattern can also be simplified: the last alternative is redundant and the 2-char-minimum of the first alternative is already covered if the trailing separator class is made optional. Suggested equivalent-but-simpler pattern (1+ alphanumerics, optional leading slash, optional internal `_ . -`, not ending in a separator):

comments.content: The filter `$lt: 1` misses documents whose (pre-migration, fraction-based) threshold is exactly `1`, which meant 100%. Those monitors keep `1`, which now means 1% under the new percent semantics — a silent data corruption that makes them almost never go down. Use `$lte: 1` (and make sure `1 * 100` yields `100`).

comments.content: `payload` is not guaranteed to be a string: lines 135-143 assign `JSON.parse(response.body)` when the content type contains `application/json`, so `payload` can be an object/array/`null`. comments.content:
`GetTooltip` is a plain render callback (not a component) but calls the `useTheme()` hook. It is invoked as `config.tooltipContent(row)` from inside `data.map(...)` in `DataTable`, so the number of hook calls depends on the number of rows. When the checks list length changes (pagination, monitor switch, resolve action) React throws "Rendered more hooks than during the previous render" and unmounts the page. Every other `useTheme` usage in this codebase sits at the top of a real component.

Fix: make the tooltip a real component, e.g. `const TooltipContent = ({ row }) => { const theme = useTheme(); ... }`, pass the component itself as `config={{ tooltipContent: TooltipContent }}`, and have `DataTable` render `React.createElement(tooltipContent, { row })` / `<TooltipContent row={row} />` instead of calling it as a function.

Default `config` object only applies when `config` is `undefined`; any caller passing a partial object silently loses all other defaults. `IncidentTable` now passes `config={{ tooltipContent: GetTooltip }}`, so `config.emptyView` becomes `undefined` and the empty-state row (line 99) renders a blank cell instead of "No data" when `data` is empty.

comments.content: The name alternative `[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.-]*[a-zA-Z0-9]` requires the value to **end** with an alphanumeric character, but Docker's own name rule is `/?[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+`, which permits names ending in `-`, `_` or `.` (e.g. `my-app-`, `app.v2.`). Such valid containers will be rejected by the form while `requestDocker` on the server would match them, so client and server validation disagree. Consider the simpler, equivalent-to-Docker pattern below (it also drops the redundant alternations).

Suggest simpler regex `/^\/?[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.-]*$/`? Wait but that would allow trailing chars — yes, that matches Docker's rule while also permitting trailing special chars. Hmm, but Docker requires at least 2 chars. Using `/^\/?[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.-]*$/` allows 1-char names, lenient — acceptable and avoids rejecting valid names.
